archetype.name: Game Manager (career backup)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup with a big arm whose Seattle job is to hit the open first read, mostly Smith-Njigba, behind a top-three defense and a run-leaning plan, not to carry the offense.

report.headline: Career-best accuracy on 51 dropbacks, propped up by Smith-Njigba and under-center looks
report.take:
Drew Lock has spent eight seasons as a strong-armed, erratic quarterback. His completion percentage over expected has been negative in all five career seasons on file, bottoming out at -6.1 with the Giants in 2024. Interceptions have followed him, including 15 in 12 games in 2020. Through two logged appearances in 2026 he looks like a different player: +6.72 CPOE (5th of 42), +0.451 EPA per dropback (3rd), zero interceptions, and 10.5 adjusted net yards per dropback. Seattle won both games, 13-10 over New England and 31-7 at Arizona.

The cause is mostly the setting, not a remade passer. He is playing a short game: 7.69 intended air yards, throws that land 1.25 yards short of the sticks on average, and only 5 of 48 attempts traveling 20+ yards. The target tree is lopsided. Jaxon Smith-Njigba drew 21 targets at +1.18 EPA each, while Rashid Shaheed's 8 targets were a net loss. The cleanest tell is formation. Under center he is 14-for-14 with an 80% success rate. From shotgun he completes 61.8%, his CPOE is -2.5, and his success rate is 37%, which looks a lot like his career baseline. The scheme is handing him easy, schemed-open throws and he is hitting them.

What the numbers hide is fragility. Fifty-one dropbacks is a tiny sample. The 1.97 EPA on deep balls comes from five throws. The 8.3% touchdown rate sits far above anything he has done before. His 12.5% bad-throw rate ranks only 18th of 32 despite the gaudy accuracy line. The better game also came against Arizona's defense, now ranked 28th, while the steadier one came against 12th-ranked New England. There is also a role question. The team's start log lists him as the starter through Week 4, but the depth chart as of October 5 lists him as QB2. Whether he takes the snaps against San Francisco is the first thing to confirm.

If he does start, expect the efficiency to come down while the shape of the plan stays the same: short, on time, Smith-Njigba-centric, with Seattle's defense keeping scores low. He is a capable caretaker in a good structure. The career record says the top-five ranks will not last.

strengths.title: Taking the schemed throws on time
strengths.body: His time to throw was 2.77 seconds in both games, and his short-area work (0-9 air yards) produced +0.52 EPA on a 59% success rate. This is the plan working as designed: get the ball out underneath and let the defense win. The approach is sustainable, though the per-play value will fall as the completion luck evens out.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba
strengths.body: Smith-Njigba has seen 21 of the 41 targets to the top five pass catchers and returned +1.18 EPA per target. Lock is winning by locking onto the best player on the field. That relationship should keep working, though defenses will start rolling coverage to him.

strengths.title: Under-center efficiency
strengths.body: He has completed all 14 under-center attempts at +0.89 EPA per play with an 80% success rate. Those are designed, defined reads, which suits a passer with his accuracy history. The perfect completion rate will not hold, but the formation will remain his friendliest look.

concerns.title: Accuracy spike against career baseline
concerns.body: His +6.72 CPOE sits against five straight negative seasons, including -5.5 in 2020 and -6.1 in 2024. From shotgun, where reads are less defined, he is at -2.5 CPOE with a 37% success rate, which is much closer to who he has been. Expect real regression toward average or below, not a new normal.

concerns.title: Small-sample touchdown and turnover luck
concerns.body: His 8.3% touchdown rate and zero interceptions come from 48 attempts, and the deep line rests on five throws. His 12.5% bad-throw rate is only middle of the pack. Interceptions have historically been part of his game, so the clean sheet is likely noise.

concerns.title: Role and supporting cast uncertainty
concerns.body: The depth chart lists him as QB2 as of October 5, even though the start log credits him with starts through Week 4. Seattle's run game is already 26th in rushing EPA, and both Jadarian Price (IR) and Zach Charbonnet (still on PUP) are out. That puts more of each drive on his arm in an offense built to lean on the run.

trend.note: Both logged games were efficient, with +6.4 and +16.1 total pass EPA. The jump in Week 2 lines up with facing Arizona's 28th-ranked defense rather than real growth. His time to throw was identical in both games and his aggressiveness rose only slightly.

nextGame.headline: Clean pocket likely, but San Francisco caps the big plays
nextGame.body:
San Francisco's defense is middling at 14th in EPA and 18th against the pass. It struggles to get home, ranking 27th in hit rate and 26th in sack rate. It is also generous underneath, 23rd in short-pass EPA allowed, which is exactly where Lock lives. The catch is that it is 2nd in explosive pass rate allowed and 4th in deep EPA, and it has held quarterbacks to 1.25 touchdowns a game (5th fewest). Expect a dink-and-dunk afternoon where drives have to be long. The other side matters too: San Francisco's offense is 1st in EPA and passing EPA, which could pull a run-leaning Seattle into throwing more than usual.

Availability tilts toward Seattle's passing game. Nick Bosa (64% of snaps) and DT James Thompson Jr. are out, which thins an already weak rush. Starting safety Marques Sigle (88% of snaps) is doubtful with a high-ankle injury, which slightly loosens the deep shell. On Seattle's side, losing Price and Charbonnet leaves the backfield thin behind a run game that was already struggling. Most important, confirm Lock is the starter given his QB2 listing.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs a soft underneath
keyMatchups.body: Lock's best area (0-9 air yards, +0.52 EPA) meets a defense ranked 23rd in short-pass EPA allowed. This is the matchup that should keep the chains moving. It also fits his low-aDOT, sticks-short tendencies.

keyMatchups.title: Weak 49ers rush minus Bosa
keyMatchups.body: San Francisco ranks 26th in sack rate even with Bosa, and Lock's line ranks 26th in hit rate allowed. With Bosa and Thompson out, Lock should see the cleaner pockets where his under-center, on-time game works best.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive plays will be scarce
keyMatchups.body: San Francisco allows the 2nd-lowest explosive pass rate, which caps the deep shots behind his inflated EPA. Sigle's absence helps a little. Still, scoring will likely require long drives and red-zone execution, and his red-zone success rate so far is just 33%.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lock or someone else takes the first snap, then how often Seattle lines up in shotgun, where his efficiency collapses to near his career norms.

restOfSeason.body:
If he holds the job, the structure stays favorable: a top-three defense, a play-caller who keeps him under center on defined reads, and Smith-Njigba drawing nearly half his looks. The per-game volume, around 24 attempts and 211 yards, is sustainable. The efficiency is not. His CPOE should drift back toward zero or below, his touchdown rate should be roughly cut in half, and interceptions should start to show up given his history. A depleted backfield until Price's estimated early-November return could force slightly more passing, which helps yardage but not efficiency.

The bigger variable is the job itself. A QB2 depth-chart listing means his weekly role could disappear without the dossier saying why. Treat any rest-of-season outlook as conditional on starting.
swingFactors: Whether he remains the starter despite the QB2 listing
Smith-Njigba's target share holding near half
Seattle's run game with Price and Charbonnet out

bets.reason: His 8.3% touchdown rate is far above any season of his career. San Francisco allows only 1.25 QB touchdowns a game (5th fewest) and the 2nd-lowest explosive pass rate. Fade the idea that the two-touchdown pace carries over.

San Francisco allows 221.8 passing yards a game, has a bottom-six pass rush now missing Bosa, and is soft underneath where Lock lives. Facing the league's top offense with a thin backfield could push his volume up. This only applies if he is confirmed as the starter.

Both of Lock's games went well under their totals (23 and 38 points against 44.5 and 40.5). Seattle's defense ranks 3rd in EPA and 2nd in deep EPA, and San Francisco's defense suppresses explosive plays. San Francisco's top-ranked offense is the risk, so this is only a slight edge.

confidence.note: Only 51 dropbacks, numbers that contradict five career seasons, and a QB2 depth-chart listing that clouds his role.
